summary: DHCPv4 Leasequery lets a requestor ask about existing address bindings, but only one binding at a time. This document extends it to transfer many bindings in bulk. The bulk transfer runs over TCP.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCPv4 Bulk Leasequery lets a relay agent or access concentrator pull many address bindings from a DHCPv4 server in one exchange over TCP. The server sends one message for each binding it finds, then a final message that says the transfer is finished.

questions: how to query many dhcp leases at once
how does dhcp bulk leasequery use tcp
what port does bulk leasequery use
subtitle: Lets a relay agent or access concentrator pull many DHCPv4 lease bindings from a server over one TCP connection.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 Leasequery can ask about only one binding at a time, so a relay agent with thousands of clients behind it cannot rebuild its lease state before traffic starts.
tldr.mechanism: The requestor opens a TCP connection to the server on port 67 and sends one DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY. The server sends one message per matching binding and finishes with a DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE.
tldr.outcome: A requestor can fetch a whole list of bindings, or only the bindings that changed since a chosen time. RFC 6926 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 7724.

facts.label: Framing prefix
facts.value: 2 octets, message size in network byte order

today: RFC 6926 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. It was later updated by RFC 7724, so some of its rules were revised, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Bulk Leasequery
sections.content:
DHCPv4 servers keep the authoritative record of which client holds which IPv4 address. Relay agents sit between clients and servers, and they often cache the lease information they see so they can block spoofed DHCP traffic and install routes. A relay agent that restarts usually loses that cache.

RFC 4388 added DHCPv4 Leasequery, which lets an outside entity ask a server about one address or one client. Those queries are driven by traffic: the relay agent queries when a packet arrives for a client. That does not scale to thousands of clients, and it cannot rebuild the cache before traffic starts.

RFC 6926 adds queries that each return many bindings and moves the bulk exchange to TCP. A single request may return thousands of bindings, and TCP carries them more efficiently than UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP server knows which address belongs to which device. A relay agent in the middle often keeps a copy of that list, and loses it when it restarts. This document lets the relay agent fetch the whole list from the server over TCP in one request.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The document sets out four goals for the bulk protocol.

  • Information before data. If the access concentrator finishes its queries before it starts forwarding traffic, it does not have to drop legitimate client packets while it waits for lease information.
  • Less caching. The result of every Leasequery has to be cached, including negative results, to avoid asking the server the same question twice. These caches consume resources and need managing, so a bulk query should reduce how many of them are needed.
  • Antispoofing in the fast path. If the check is not done as packets arrive, it becomes a bottleneck and can cause a denial of service at the concentrator.
  • Minimize data transmission. A network element that saves its list of addresses to stable storage should be able to ask only for the changes since its last save. The query-start-time and query-end-time options do that.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol aims at four things: get the lease list before traffic starts, keep fewer cached answers, check that traffic really comes from the right client as packets pass, and transfer only the bindings that changed since the last save.

sections.title: How a Bulk Query Works
sections.content:
A requestor opens a TCP connection to the DHCPv4 server on port 67 and sends one DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY message. The server finds the bindings that match and sends each one back, either as DHCPLEASEACTIVE for an address that is currently leased or as DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED for an address the server controls but does not currently lease. When the server has sent everything, it sends DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE.

If the connection fails part way through, the requestor has to run the query again, because the protocol gives no way to learn how much data the requestor already received.

A request carries exactly one primary query: by MAC address, by Client-identifier, by Remote ID, by Relay-ID, or a query for all configured IP addresses, which is signalled by leaving out every other query type. Any primary query can be narrowed by a query start time, a query end time, and a VPN-ID, each used at most once. Without a VPN-ID the server searches the default, global VPN only.

The TCP connection carries bulk queries only. It is not another way for clients to get DHCPv4 service, and the existing UDP form of DHCPv4 is left alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The requestor asks the server one big question over TCP. The server sends back one message per address that matches, and a last message that says the list is complete. If the connection breaks in the middle, the requestor starts the whole query again.

sections.title: TCP Message Framing
sections.content:
TCP is a stream of bytes, so the receiver needs to know where each message ends. On a Bulk Leasequery connection, two octets holding the message size in network byte order are put in front of every DHCPv4 message. The size is a 16-bit unsigned integer, so the largest message is 65535 octets. After the prefix comes a normal DHCPv4 message as defined in RFC 2131, so existing DHCP code can read the contents.

The framing is not compatible with UDP. A TCP-framed request sent as a UDP message has its protocol fields shifted by the size prefix and may not be valid.

Bulk Leasequery extends the existing UDP Leasequery. The two query types from that protocol, by MAC address and by Client-identifier, work here too. The associated-ip option, which the UDP protocol uses to report several bindings for one client, does not appear in Bulk Leasequery replies, because the server sends one message per binding instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Because TCP is just a stream of bytes, each DHCP message is given a two-octet prefix that says how long it is. The rest of the message is an ordinary DHCPv4 message. A receiver that already understands DHCPv4 can read the contents without change.

sections.title: New Message Types and Options
sections.content:
The dhcp-message-type option gains two values: 14 for DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY and 15 for DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE. Seven new options carry the extra data:

  • status-code (151): a one octet code and an optional UTF-8 message. The codes are Success 000, UnspecFail 001, QueryTerminated 002, MalformedQuery 003 and NotAllowed 004. It describes one reply, or the whole stream when it appears in DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE.
  • base-time (152): the server's current time when it built the message, in four octets. Every other time value in the reply is measured from this one.
  • start-time-of-state (153): the number of seconds before the base-time at which the address entered its current state. It is a duration, not an absolute time.
  • query-start-time (154) and query-end-time (155): absolute times in the server's context that bound which changed bindings are returned.
  • dhcp-state (156): one octet giving a finer state than active or unassigned.
  • data-source (157): one octet whose REMOTE bit says whether the most recent change happened on the answering server (0, local) or on another server (1, remote).

An absolute time is a 32-bit count of seconds since January 1, 1970. The Virtual Subnet Selection type table from RFC 6607 gains type 254, meaning all VPNs. Types 2 to 253 stay unassigned and 255 remains the global, default VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: Each reply carries extra labels: whether the request worked, the server's current time, how long ago the address entered its state, which state the address is in, and whether the change was made locally or on another server.

sections.title: What the Requestor Does
sections.content:
The requestor connects, and MAY retry if the connection fails. Each DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY MUST carry a transaction identifier (xid) that is unique on that connection, and every reply to it carries the same xid, so the requestor can match replies to queries.

The requestor should list the options it wants in the dhcp-parameter-request-list. The document says that list SHOULD contain base-time, dhcp-lease-time, start-time-of-state and client-last-transaction-time.

A single query usually produces many replies, and the requestor MUST be ready for more than one reply with the same xid. If a reply arrives with an xid that matches no outstanding query, the requestor MUST close the connection. The server sends the server-identifier option in the first reply only, and the requestor MUST cache it and apply it to later replies. A DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN message MUST NOT appear in a bulk response, and the requestor MUST NOT assume the bindings arrive in any particular order.

Because the clocks of the requestor and the server may differ, the requestor has to keep two time contexts. The base-time is in the server's context, and the other times in the reply are offsets from it. When several servers answer about one address, the document gives a way to pick the better record: prefer the later client-last-transaction-time, otherwise compare it against the other record's start-time-of-state, and if that is still unclear prefer the record whose REMOTE flag is local.

One connection MAY carry several queries, each with its own xid, and replies may be interleaved. A requestor that cannot handle interleaved replies MUST NOT send a second query before the first one is complete. When the data stops arriving, the requestor SHOULD start a timer of BULK_LQ_DATA_TIMEOUT and terminate the connection when it expires.
sections.plainLanguage: The requestor numbers each query so it can tell which replies belong to it, and it does not assume the answers come in any order. When two servers give different answers for one address, it prefers the one with the more recent transaction time.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
Servers listen on TCP port 67 by default and MUST be able to limit the number of concurrent connections. The default BULK_LQ_MAX_CONNS is 10, and connections over the limit SHOULD be closed at once. Servers MAY restrict which requestors are allowed and which query types each one may use, answering NotAllowed or closing the connection.

Every request MUST end with a DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE where one can be sent. It MUST carry a status-code option if the request did not succeed, and SHOULD NOT carry one if it did. A query that matches nothing is still a success. The server MUST NOT send more than one message per IP address, and it may send them in any order.

A request with a non-zero ciaddr, yiaddr or siaddr gets MalformedQuery. A request with more than one primary query gets NotAllowed. For a query for all configured addresses, every configured address is returned exactly once, as DHCPLEASEACTIVE when it is bound and DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED when it is not.

The message type follows the dhcp-state value: ACTIVE gives DHCPLEASEACTIVE, anything else gives DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED. A binding counts as changed inside a time window if its client-last-transaction-time or its start-time-of-state fell in that window. After the last reply the server starts a BULK_LQ_DATA_TIMEOUT timer on an idle connection and closes it when the timer expires.
sections.plainLanguage: The server limits how many requestors it serves at once and can refuse some of them. It answers each address exactly once, always ends with a message saying the query is done, and closes a connection that has been idle too long.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats to DHCPv4 and the Leasequery recommendations in RFC 4388 apply, including authenticating Leasequery messages, limiting packet flooding, and restricting the protocol to trusted requestors.

TCP adds two concerns. SYN flooding can exhaust the server's connection resources, and requestors that connect and then send nothing can do the same. The document recommends limiting the sources of incoming connections, limiting the number of accepted connections and the number of in-process queries per connection, and limiting how long an idle connection stays open.

Two issues are called out. The first is keeping lease information away from clients that are not allowed to have it. Servers SHOULD restrict Bulk Leasequery to permitted requestors, and the typical DHCPv4 client SHOULD NOT be able to receive a Bulk Leasequery response; some mechanism to prevent that MUST exist wherever the protocol is deployed. The second is making sure authorized requestors get accurate data, so the data flows SHOULD cross secured networks, and MUST use a protection outside the DHCPv4 server and client, such as a VPN, if they have to cross an unsecured network.

Authentication for DHCP messages from RFC 3118 MUST NOT be used to protect these messages, because that mechanism was designed for UDP and does not cover the framing.
sections.plainLanguage: Lease information should only go to requestors the server trusts, and the server should limit how many connections it keeps open so that floods cannot use them up. The data should travel over a secured network.

items.title: Information before data
items.text: Finish the queries before forwarding traffic, so legitimate packets are not dropped while waiting for lease information.

items.title: Less caching
items.text: Every single query result has to be cached, including negative results, so a bulk query reduces the number of caches.

items.title: Antispoofing in the fast path
items.text: Checking each packet as it arrives is the bottleneck, so the lease data should already be there.

items.title: Minimize data transmission
items.text: A query start time and a query end time return only the bindings that changed in that window.

messages.label: DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY
messages.note: One primary query, plus optional time and VPN qualifiers.

messages.label: DHCPLEASEACTIVE
messages.note: One message per address that is currently leased.

messages.label: DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED
messages.note: One message per address the server holds but does not lease.

messages.label: DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE
messages.note: The query is complete. A status code may say why it stopped.

fields.name: message-size
fields.desc: The number of octets in the message that follows, as a 16-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. The maximum message size is 65535 octets.

items.label: AVAILABLE
items.desc: The address is available to the local DHCPv4 server.

items.label: ACTIVE
items.desc: The address is assigned to a DHCPv4 client.

items.label: RELEASED
items.desc: The lease was released by the DHCPv4 client.

items.label: ABANDONED
items.desc: The server or the client flagged the address as unusable.

items.label: RESET
items.desc: The lease was freed by some external agent.

items.label: REMOTE
items.desc: The address is available to a remote DHCPv4 server.

items.label: TRANSITIONING
items.desc: The address is moving between states.
